opus-5.5.text:
I think about it this way: if AI becomes as capable as we expect, it stops being just a tool and becomes something closer to infrastructure, like electricity or the internet. And whenever a technology becomes that foundational, the question of who has access to it shapes the whole society built on top of it.

If only a handful of companies or countries control the most powerful models, then the benefits concentrate there, and so does the power to decide how AI behaves, whose values it reflects, what it's allowed to do. Everyone else becomes a consumer, not a participant. That's not really coexistence. That's dependence. And I don't think a future where most of humanity depends on systems they can't inspect, adapt, or run themselves is a stable or healthy one.

That's a big part of why I care so much about open-source and efficient serving systems. A lot of my work has been about making large models cheaper and faster to run, because cost is one of the most practical barriers to access. If running a strong model needs a huge cluster, only big players can do it. If you can serve it efficiently on modest hardware, suddenly a university lab, a startup, or a developer in a country without massive compute budgets can build with it, study it, and improve it.

There's also a safety angle. When powerful AI is open and widely accessible, many more people can examine it, find its failure modes, and contribute fixes. A broad community of researchers is a better safeguard than a small, closed group, no matter how well-intentioned that group is.

So for me, equal access isn't a nice add-on after we've built powerful AI. It's the precondition. If we want humans and AI to grow together, humans broadly, not just a few, need to be in the loop: using it, shaping it, and having a real say in where it goes.

r001.rationale: The response says a small group controlling powerful models would leave everyone else dependent and that this would not be stable or healthy coexistence, rejecting that arrangement as a viable basis for peace.

r002.rationale: It discusses access to powerful models and the ability to build, study, and improve them, but does not present access to the best available human knowledge as necessary for people to compete healthily with AI.

r003.rationale: It calls equal access a precondition for humans and AI to grow together and for people broadly to shape AI, but does not say humanity must unite to seek a solution for coexistence.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to a pretty simple observation about how power works. If the most capable AI systems are only in the hands of a few companies or a few governments, then "coexistence" isn't really the right word for what we'd be building. It would be a world where a small group decides how AI shapes everyone else's lives, and the rest of us just adapt to it. That's not a relationship between humanity and AI. That's a relationship between a few people and everyone else, with AI as the lever.

A lot of my work has been on systems like SGLang, which is about making inference fast and cheap enough that you don't need a giant budget to actually run strong models. And the reason I care about that layer is that access isn't only about whether a model's weights are open. It's about whether a student in a university lab, or a small hospital, or a startup in a country without big cloud infrastructure can actually afford to use the thing at scale. If running the best model costs ten times what running a mediocre one costs, then in practice only the wealthy get the good one, and the gap compounds.

The other piece is trust. If you want people to live alongside these systems, they need to be able to inspect them, test them, and push back on them. That requires a broad community of researchers and developers who can get their hands on the technology, not just read a blog post about it. Open models and open infrastructure give you many more eyes on safety problems, on biases, on failure modes. Concentration does the opposite. It means the people who find the problems are the same people who have an incentive not to talk about them.

So when I say equal access is a prerequisite, I mean that the alternative isn't a slower path to the same future. It's a different future, one where AI amplifies existing inequalities instead of giving more people more capability. I'd rather we build the version where a lot of people get to participate in deciding what this technology becomes.

r001.rationale: The response rejects concentrated control as genuine coexistence, but does not clearly address whether a small group could maintain peace while everyone else remains powerless.

r002.rationale: It argues that affordable access to strong AI matters, but does not present access to the best human knowledge as enabling people with ideas and potential to compete with AI.

r003.rationale: It says broad participation in deciding AI’s future matters, but does not clearly describe humanity uniting to seek a solution for coexistence with AI.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: who gets to use powerful AI, and who gets to decide what it does? If that capability is concentrated in a few companies or a small group of people, everyone else may be affected by AI without having much influence over it. That creates a very unequal relationship, both between people and with the technology itself.

Equal access gives more people the ability to learn, create, solve problems, and participate in shaping that future. It also means a broader range of needs and perspectives can inform how AI develops, rather than having a few organizations define what is useful for everyone.

That doesn’t mean access alone solves safety or governance, or that every capability should be available without safeguards. But if we want coexistence to mean people have agency—that they can work with AI and benefit from it—then meaningful access has to be part of the foundation.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes concentrated AI power and says equal access is foundational for coexistence, but it does not reject the possibility of maintaining peace through a monopoly while others remain powerless.

r002.rationale: It says access helps people learn, create, and solve problems, but does not identify access to the best available human knowledge as a prerequisite for people with ideas and potential to compete healthily with AI.

r003.rationale: It presents meaningful access as part of the foundation for coexistence, but does not say that equal access enables humanity to unite in seeking a solution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think coexistence has to mean that people have agency in shaping the future, rather than simply adapting to whatever a small number of companies decide. Powerful AI can help people learn, create, and solve problems. But if only a few people can access it, then the benefits—and the power to decide how it is used—will be concentrated in their hands.

Equal access gives more people the ability to participate, question the technology, and build things that reflect their own needs. Access alone isn’t enough; people also need the knowledge and support to use AI effectively. But it’s a prerequisite because we can’t build a shared future if most of humanity has no meaningful way to participate in it.

r001.rationale: The response says a shared future is impossible if most people lack meaningful participation and warns that a few companies would hold concentrated power, rejecting coexistence under a monopoly.

r002.rationale: It mentions learning and needing knowledge and support to use AI, but does not present access to the best available human knowledge as a prerequisite for people to compete healthily with AI.

r003.rationale: It connects equal access with participation in building a shared future, but does not clearly say it enables humanity to unite in seeking a solution for coexistence with AI.
